name_en: Aged White Tea Cake (Lao Bai Cha)
cultivar: Fuding Dabai, Fuding Dahao, Zhenghe Dabai and Cai Cha
processing: Withered-and-dried white tea (mostly Shou Mei and Gong Mei, sometimes Mudan or Yin Zhen) that is steamed, pressed into cakes and slowly dried, then stored for years in dry, odour-free conditions while it oxidises and sweetens slowly.
harvest_season: Made from spring or autumn leaf of the pressing year; what matters at sale is the year on the wrapper, not the season.
appearance_dry: A compressed disc of large brown, amber and olive leaves with stems, darkening and loosening with age.
appearance_liquor: Amber to orange-red, bright and clear; never black or muddy.
appearance_wet: Big brown-olive leaves that are still supple and whole, not mushy.
taste_profile: Honey, dried dates and jujube, warm wood and a soft herbal-medicinal sweetness, thick and smooth with no bitterness and a long warming finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, gaiwan or clay pot; rinse once. After the gongfu session, simmer the spent leaves in a pot for ten minutes for one last rich cup, or simmer fresh chunks from the start in winter.

vintage_note: Sold strictly by year: the market is mostly cakes pressed from about 2010 onwards, with 3–5 years common, 7–10 years premium and genuine pre-2008 cakes rare and expensive. The slogan 'one year tea, three years medicine, seven years treasure' is marketing, not a rule. Backdated wrappers are common, so judge by the cup: amber liquor, supple leaf, date-and-honey aroma, no mustiness.
description:
Lao Bai Cha, 'old white tea', is white tea that has been pressed into cakes and left to age, and it is one of the big stories of recent Chinese tea. Fujian producers, watching pu-erh prices, began pressing their cheap leafy whites (Shou Mei and Gong Mei above all, sometimes Mudan and even Yin Zhen) into pu-erh-style discs, by the usual rough estimate in the late 2000s, and the market for cakes with a year on the wrapper grew from there.

The pressing is gentle: the dried white tea is softened with steam, pressed into a disc and dried slowly again. Then time does the rest. White tea is never fired or rolled, so its enzymes are only sleeping, and in a dry, clean store the leaf oxidises slowly, sugars develop and the hay-and-flower freshness turns toward dates, honey and wood. It does not need humidity the way pu-erh does; it needs dryness and no smells.

A good aged cake pours amber, not black, and tastes of honey, jujube and warm wood, with the herbal sweetness the Chinese call 'medicinal' and a thick, smooth texture that cannot be made bitter. Brew it with boiling water in a gaiwan or clay pot, rinse once, and expect eight steeps; then simmer the spent leaves for a last rich cup. In winter, simmering fresh chunks from the start in a glass kettle is the way most Fujian drinkers take it.

Buying needs scepticism. Most honest cakes on the market are three to seven years old; ten-year-old cakes are a premium niche; a cake said to be pressed before the late 2000s is suspect, because few people were pressing white tea then. Wrappers are backdated freely. The checks: the liquor should be amber and bright, the wet leaf supple and whole, the smell of dates and honey rather than damp or smoke, and the price should rise sharply with age rather than being suspiciously flat. 'One year tea, three years medicine, seven years treasure' is a slogan; the real improvement is gradual and depends on storage.

The cheapest, safest route is to buy young Shou Mei cakes from a seller you trust and age them yourself; five years later you will have the real thing and know exactly what it is.
sources_note: Dates for the start of widespread white-tea pressing ('late 2000s', 'from about 2010') are approximate and based on market history rather than a documented first pressing.
history:
White tea was mainly an export product, and it drew attention in Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou only recently; aged white tea as something to collect belongs to that turn. Little is documented about when pressing white tea into cakes first became common; the late 2000s is the usual rough estimate, not a recorded start.

By the early 2010s the market was clearly there. At a 2011 auction during the Yuyuan tea festival in Shanghai, a 375 g Fuding cake described as twenty years old reportedly sold for 188,000 yuan, and press reports in 2014 described Fuding white tea rising in price while other premium teas fell. The age of such a cake rests on the seller's word, so treat it as a sign of the market rather than as proof of old pressing.
